276213069_0480b48f.text: There are at least 2 genetically distinguishable subtypes of tuberoinfundibular A12 neurons: those expressing the dopamine transporter (DAT) and the prolactin receptor (PRLR) (18). Traditionally, A12 neurons express tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), which catalyzes the conversion of l-tyrosine to l-DOPA, and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), which converts l-DOPA to dopamine. However, these neurons lack dopamine beta hydroxylase, the enzyme required to convert dopamine to norepinephrine, a feature shared by all central dopaminergic neurons. Developmentally, the DA phenotype in A12 neurons emerges early, and these neurons are among the first hypothalamic neurons to express TH and AADC (4)

276213069_161ba639.text: This review highlights the diverse origins, mechanisms, and physiological roles of tuberoinfundibular dopaminergic A12 neurons in the arcuate nucleus and median eminence, emphasizing their essential role in prolactin regulation and broader influences on growth hormone, metabolism, and hypothalamic development.

276213069_66d9eaa4.text: A12 neurons, also known as the tuberoinfundibular dopaminergic (TIDA) neurons, are predominately found in the dorsomedial subdivision of the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARC) (9). Their long axons project to the external layer of the median eminence, where they release dopamine from neurosecretory terminals into the hypothalamo-pituitary portal blood vessels (10, 11). This process is critically dependent on prolactin itself, which stimulates TIDA neurons to secrete dopamine. In turn, this dopamine travels through the portal blood system to the anterior pituitary, where it binds to dopamine D2 receptors on lactotrophs, suppressing prolactin secretion in a negative feedback loop (7, 8)

276213069_1bb46f85.text: .The developmental trajectory and maturation of A12 neurons have recently garnered attention. In rodents, TH-positive cells first appear in the ventral diencephalon around embryonic day 11, with the eventual A12 neurons developing from proliferative Sox2- and Sox9-positive tanycyte-like cells lining the ventral third ventricle (17, 18). These embryonic precursors are generated under the influence of signaling molecules such as fibroblast growth factor 8b and bone morphogenetic proteins, and they migrate radially into the hypothalamic parenchyma to form the mature arcuate nucleus architecture (17, 18)

276213069_4dd85bc2.text: .In rodents, A12 neurons are functionally and anatomically segregated into 3 primary groups: the rostral, middle, and caudal subpopulations (Fig. 1) (26, 27). The rostral and middle groups project to the intermediate and neural lobe of the pituitary, while the caudal A12 population specifically innervates the external zone of the median eminence (26, 28). This anatomical distinction corresponds with differences in prolactin responsiveness and hormonal regulation. Specifically, the rostral and middle groups express the prolactin receptor and exhibit activation in response to prolactin, whereas the caudal group largely does not, yet still contributes to feedback regulation (27, 29). Transcriptomic analyses have also revealed molecular heterogeneity among arcuate dopamine neurons, suggesting that these subgroups may differ in gene expression profiles and signaling properties (30, 31)

276213069_2798d76f.text: .Furthermore, male and female A12 neurons differ markedly in their transcriptomic profiles and electrophysiological responses. Although estrogen and prolactin activate similar intracellular pathways in both sexes, the baseline firing properties and inhibitory responses to dopamine D2 receptor agonists differ in sexually dimorphic patterns (31, 33)

276213069_1a5074a3.text: .transcriptomic analyses suggest that A12 neurons are not a homogeneous population. Distinct subsets can be identified based on gene expression profiles, prolactin sensitivity, and projection targets (30, 31). These findings raise the possibility that some A12 neurons may participate in local hypothalamic signaling or broader neuroendocrine regulation beyond the median eminence

276213069_aff34d62.text: .Single-cell RNA sequencing and anatomical mapping studies have identified at least 3 distinct molecular subgroups of A12 neurons, each characterized by differential expression of ion channels, neurotransmitter receptors, and neuropeptides (30, 31). Some subsets coexpress markers associated with GABAergic transmission, while others are more selectively dopaminergic, suggesting functional specialization. In female mice, prolactin receptor expression is enriched in rostral and middle A12 neurons, whereas in males this pattern is less pronounced, indicating sex-specific molecular organization (31)

276213069_6a4befb9.text: .In recent years, the use of single-cell transcriptomics, Cre driver lines, and viral tracing tools has begun to refine our understanding of A12 neuron heterogeneity. Distinct molecularly defined subpopulations have now been identified within the rostral, middle, and caudal ARC, differing in expression of prolactin receptor, vesicular GABA transporter, and peptide cotransmitters (30, 31). These subtypes may differentially influence not only prolactin release but also local hypothalamic circuits involved in feeding, growth, and reproductive regulation.
